grammar_topic: Present Simple and Present Continuous; action and state verbs
title: Sunday Lunch
body: Every Sunday, my grandmother cooks a huge lunch for the whole family, and everyone always finds an excuse to be there. She believes cooking is the best way to show love, so she never lets anyone leave the table hungry. Right now, she's stirring a pot of soup while my uncle argues loudly with my father about football, as usual. My cousin, who is famously stubborn, insists on helping in the kitchen even though nobody wants his help. 'I know exactly how much salt this needs,' he says confidently, reaching for the salt before my grandmother stops him. She doesn't trust him with seasoning — not since the disastrous rice incident two years ago. My little sister, who is shy around most adults, is completely relaxed here, laughing at my uncle's terrible jokes. Meanwhile, my mother is setting the table, counting plates twice because someone always forgets to mention a last-minute guest. Today, we're expecting my aunt and her new husband, who nobody has properly met yet. My grandmother wants everything perfect, though she'd never admit she's nervous. As the smell of fresh bread fills the kitchen, I realise these loud, chaotic Sundays are exactly what I'll miss most when I eventually move out.

words.context: My cousin, who is famously stubborn.
He says confidently, reaching for the salt.
She doesn't trust him with seasoning.
The disastrous rice incident two years ago.
My little sister, who is shy around most adults.
Forgets to mention a last-minute guest.

grammar_topic: future forms: Present Continuous, be going to, will/won't
title: The Big Family Trip
body: Next summer, my parents are finally taking the whole family to the coast, something we've talked about for years. My father has already booked the hotel, so this time it's really going to happen. 'We're leaving on the first of July,' he announced last week, showing everyone the confirmation email. My little brother, who's terrified of long car journeys, immediately asked if we're flying instead. 'No, we're driving,' my mother said, 'it'll be an adventure.' I think he'll complain the whole way, honestly, but nobody's telling him that yet. My sister is going to bring her boyfriend this year, which makes things a little more complicated — where will everyone sleep? My mother's already going to rearrange the whole plan around it. I'll probably spend most of the trip reading on the beach, while my father will insist on visiting every historical site nearby, whether we want to or not. My grandmother, surprisingly, says she'll join us too, despite hating long journeys. 'I won't miss this trip,' she said firmly. Looking at everyone's excitement, I suspect this will be a trip none of us forgets, for better or worse.

words.context: Taking the whole family to the coast.
Going to rearrange the whole plan.
My father will insist on visiting every site.
I suspect this will be a trip none forgets.

grammar_topic: Present Perfect and Past Simple
title: The News from Amira
body: Amira called me yesterday with news I never expected. She's finished her degree, passed her final exams last month, and already found a job in the city. 'I've never worked so hard in my life,' she told me, laughing with relief. I remember when we studied together years ago; she barely passed her first-year exams and nearly gave up twice. Since then, she's changed enormously. Last year, she moved to a new city alone, which took real courage. She's saved enough money now to rent her own flat, something neither of us imagined back then. 'Have you told your parents yet?' I asked. 'I called them right after the interview,' she said, still sounding amazed at her own luck. We talked about our old university, and she admitted she visited it briefly last spring, just to see how much it had changed. I felt genuinely proud of her, remembering the exhausted, anxious student she used to be. Now she sounded confident, almost unrecognisable. Before hanging up, she promised to visit soon. I've already started planning what to cook, though knowing Amira, she'll probably bring the food herself, just like always.

words.context: Enough money to rent her own flat.
Still sounding amazed at her own luck.
She admitted she visited it briefly.
The exhausted, anxious student she used to be.

grammar_topic: Present Perfect + for and since; Present Perfect Continuous
title: Building the House
body: My parents have been building their house for almost four years now, and it still isn't finished. They've been saving money since before I was born, buying materials whenever they could afford them. 'We've been doing this room by room,' my father explains, slightly embarrassed, whenever guests ask. He's been working every weekend since spring, laying tiles in the kitchen himself to save money. My mother has been choosing paint colours for months, changing her mind constantly. She's been dreaming of a garden since they bought the land, though right now it's just dirt and a few determined weeds. 'How long have you been living without a proper roof?' my aunt asked recently, only half joking. Actually, the roof has been finished for two years — it's the inside that's still work in progress. I've been helping whenever I visit, mostly painting walls badly while my father laughs at my technique. Despite the mess, there's something exciting about watching a house slowly become a home. My parents have waited so long for this that I think they'll miss the building process itself, once it's finally, truly done.

words.context: Buying materials whenever they could afford them.
Laying tiles in the kitchen himself.
Just dirt and a few determined weeds.
It's the inside that's still work in progress.
My father laughs at my technique.

grammar_topic: choosing between the comparative and superlative
title: The Fastest Way Home
body: Every evening, I face the same decision: which is the quickest way home — the metro, the bus, or a taxi? The metro is usually the most reliable option, though it's also the most crowded during rush hour. The bus is cheaper than the metro, but it's definitely the slowest, especially when traffic is bad. Yesterday, I decided to try the new express bus, which the company claims is faster than the ordinary route. It wasn't much quicker, honestly, though the seats were more comfortable than the old buses. My colleague insists that taxis are the most convenient option, but they're also the most expensive by far, and I can't afford one every day. My neighbour, who's a lot more patient than me, prefers cycling; she says it's healthier and cheaper than any other option. Personally, I think the metro remains the safest choice in bad weather, even if it's not the most pleasant experience during summer heat. Tonight, though, with rain pouring outside, the decision is easy — the metro, however crowded, is clearly the better option compared to waiting for a bus that might never arrive.

words.context: The most crowded during rush hour.
Taxis are the most convenient option.
I can't afford one every day.
Who's a lot more patient than me.

grammar_topic: articles: a/an, the, and zero article
title: A Museum, The Museum
body: Yesterday, I visited a museum I'd never been to before, tucked away on a quiet street downtown. The museum was smaller than I expected, but the collection inside was genuinely impressive. At the entrance, a guide handed me a map and explained that the building itself used to be a factory. 'The factory closed in the nineties,' she said, 'and the city later turned it into a cultural centre.' Inside, I saw a painting that immediately caught my attention — the painting showed a busy street scene from a hundred years ago. Nearby, an old photograph showed the same street exactly as it looks today, barely changed at all. I generally prefer modern art, but this particular collection focused mostly on local history, which surprised me pleasantly. A group of schoolchildren moved noisily from room to room, clearly more interested in the gift shop than the exhibits. Near the exit, there was a small café where I had a coffee before leaving. The coffee wasn't especially memorable, but the view of the old courtyard through the window definitely was. I've decided the museum deserves a second, quieter visit sometime soon.

words.context: Tucked away on a quiet street.
The collection inside was genuinely impressive.
The building used to be a factory.
Turned it into a cultural centre.
A painting that immediately caught my attention.
More interested in the gift shop than the exhibits.

grammar_topic: obligation and prohibition: have to, must, should
title: Office Phone Rules
body: On my first day at the new office, my manager explained the phone rules carefully. 'You mustn't use personal phones during meetings,' she said, 'but you don't have to switch them off completely.' Employees have to answer client calls within three rings, according to company policy. I must admit, I found this rule stricter than my last job. 'You should always introduce yourself clearly,' she added, 'callers get frustrated when they can't understand who they're speaking to.' We mustn't transfer calls without explaining why, something I learned the hard way during my first confusing week. My colleague, who's worked here for years, told me I don't have to worry too much — most callers are patient if you're polite. Still, I must remember never to eat while on a call; apparently, a client once complained about hearing someone chewing. Employees should also keep calls brief when the office is busy, though nobody enforces this strictly. By the end of my first week, I'd memorised most of the rules, though I still occasionally forget that I mustn't put anyone on hold for more than a minute without checking back.

words.context: Employees have to answer client calls.
We mustn't transfer calls without explaining why.
Most callers are patient if you're polite.
I mustn't put anyone on hold for more than a minute.

grammar_topic: ability and possibility: can, could, be able to
title: Learning to Fix Phones
body: My neighbour can fix almost any broken phone, a skill he taught himself after years of curiosity. When I was younger, he could barely change a lightbulb without help, so his transformation genuinely surprises everyone on our street. 'Anyone can learn this,' he insists, though I'm not convinced I'd ever be able to open a phone without breaking it completely. Last month, despite having no proper tools, he was able to repair my cracked screen in under an hour. He says phones can be surprisingly simple once you understand the basic parts inside. I could probably learn the theory, he thinks, but my hands aren't steady enough for the delicate work. 'You'll be able to do this too, with practice,' he encourages, handing me a tiny screwdriver. I try, nervously, and somehow manage to remove one screw without disaster. Apparently, this counts as progress. He couldn't afford proper training when he started, so he learned everything from online videos instead. Now people from the whole neighbourhood bring him their broken phones, and he can usually fix them for far less than the shop charges. I might not become an expert, but I'm definitely able to appreciate the skill now.

words.context: A skill he taught himself after years of curiosity.
I'm not convinced I'd ever be able to.
I could probably learn the theory.

grammar_topic: past tenses: simple, continuous and perfect
title: The Final Match
body: By the time the whistle blew for half-time, our team had already scored twice, though nobody had expected such a strong start. We had been training every day for a month, and it was finally paying off. While the coach was giving instructions during the break, I noticed the opposing captain watching us nervously from across the pitch. They had lost their best player to injury the previous week, which had clearly affected their confidence. As the second half began, I was running down the wing when someone passed me the ball unexpectedly. I hadn't practised that particular move much, but somehow it worked perfectly. The crowd was cheering loudly by the time I scored, and for a moment, everything else disappeared. We had worked so hard for this moment that when the final whistle went, several teammates were crying with relief. Afterwards, our coach admitted she had been secretly worried all week, though she'd hidden it well. As we celebrated, I realised this was the proudest I had felt in years, and probably would for a long time afterwards.

words.context: By the time the whistle blew.
Watching us nervously from across the pitch.
Lost their best player to injury.
I was running down the wing.
Someone passed me the ball unexpectedly.

grammar_topic: past and present habits: used to, usually
title: We Used to Argue About Everything
body: My brother and I used to argue about absolutely everything when we were teenagers — music, chores, even which channel to watch. These days, we usually agree on most things, though we still disagree loudly about football teams. We used to share a room, which honestly made the arguments worse; now we usually only see each other at family dinners. He used to borrow my clothes without asking, something that used to make me furious. Nowadays, he usually asks first, though he still occasionally forgets. Our relationship used to feel competitive, like we were always comparing grades or achievements. Now we usually support each other instead, especially since he moved to another city for work. I used to think we'd never get along properly as adults, but I was wrong. We usually call each other every weekend now, something neither of us used to bother doing. Our mother, who used to referee our childhood fights constantly, says she's relieved we finally act like friends. Looking back, I think we used to fight simply because we were too similar, and similar people, apparently, usually clash before they eventually understand each other.

words.context: We used to argue about everything.
Music, chores, even which channel to watch.

Our relationship used to feel competitive.

grammar_topic: the passive (all tenses)
title: How the Film Was Made
body: The film was shot over eighteen months in three different countries, though most scenes were filmed in an old studio outside the city. The script was written by a first-time director, which surprised many critics once the film was finally released. Every costume was designed by hand, and the main character's coat, in particular, was praised widely by fashion magazines. The soundtrack was composed by a young musician who was discovered almost by accident at a small concert. Several difficult scenes were shot at night to capture the right lighting, which meant the crew was often exhausted by morning. The lead actress was chosen from hundreds of candidates after a long audition process. Interestingly, the film's final scene was completely rewritten just weeks before shooting ended. Once the film was completed, it was shown at several festivals before being officially released worldwide. Reviews were generally positive, though some critics felt the ending was left too open. Millions of tickets have since been sold, and the film is now being studied in several film schools as an example of unusual, effective storytelling.

words.context: The script was written by a first-time director.
Every costume was designed by hand.
The soundtrack was composed by a young musician.
The crew was often exhausted by morning.
The final scene was completely rewritten.

grammar_topic: modal verbs of deduction: might, can't, must
title: Where's Farrukh?
body: Farrukh hasn't come to work for three days, and nobody seems to know exactly why. 'He must be sick,' says one colleague, 'he looked pale on Friday.' Someone else disagrees. 'He can't be sick — he posted photos from the mountains yesterday.' His phone might be broken, another suggests, since nobody's calls are going through. His desk still has his coffee cup from Friday, untouched, which seems strange if he'd planned to be away. 'He might have told the manager privately,' someone offers, though the manager looks equally confused when asked. His neighbour mentioned seeing him loading a suitcase into his car early Monday morning — he must have left in a hurry, though nobody knows where. 'He can't have quit without telling anyone,' his closest friend insists, though even she seems uncertain now. The mountain photos could have been posted automatically, someone points out, from an old scheduled post. By Thursday afternoon, everyone has a different theory, each equally uncertain. When Farrukh finally walks in on Friday, tired but smiling, explaining a sudden family emergency, half the office admits they'd already imagined much stranger explanations.

words.context: His coffee cup from Friday, untouched.
He might have told the manager privately.
Loading a suitcase into his car.
He must have left in a hurry.
He can't have quit without telling anyone.

grammar_topic: first conditional and future time clauses with when, until
title: After the Exams
body: If I pass all my final exams this year, I'll finally apply to study architecture at university. My parents keep asking what I'll do when the results come out, and honestly, I don't fully know yet. If my grades are good enough, I'll move to the capital for my studies, though I'll miss home more than I expect to admit. Until the results arrive next month, I'm trying not to think about it too much, though it's difficult. As soon as I know my results, I'll call my grandmother first — she's the one who always believed I'd get here. If I don't get the grades I need, I'll probably retake one exam in the autumn instead of giving up completely. My best friend says that when we both finish school, we'll travel somewhere together before starting university, if our parents allow it. Until then, we're both studying every evening, quizzing each other on outdated notes. If everything goes well, this time next year I'll be living in a small student flat, surrounded by unfamiliar streets and, hopefully, new friends. Whatever happens, I'll always remember these last uncertain weeks of school.

words.context: Apply to study architecture at university.
I'll finally apply to study architecture.
If my grades are good enough.
Quizzing each other on outdated notes.
These last uncertain weeks of school.

grammar_topic: second conditional; choosing between the first and second conditional
title: If We Had a Bigger House
body: If we had a bigger house, my mother always says, she'd finally have a proper garden instead of three pots on the balcony. My father disagrees; he thinks if they moved somewhere larger, they'd just fill it with more unnecessary things. If I had my own place, I'd probably paint every wall a different colour, something my mother would never allow here. My sister, more practical than either of us, says if she designed a house from scratch, she'd build it with fewer stairs and more sunlight. We often imagine what we'd do if we won enough money to build our dream home. I'd add a small library, if space weren't an issue, filled with every book I've never had room for. My father, surprisingly sentimental for once, said if he built a new house, he'd keep our old front door — the one with our childhood height marks pencilled on it. My mother would probably cry, if that door somehow survived a house move. Realistically, none of this will happen anytime soon, but on quiet evenings, imagining our impossible dream house feels like its own small kind of comfort.

words.context: Fill it with more unnecessary things.
My sister, more practical than either of us.
If she designed a house from scratch.
Our childhood height marks pencilled on it.

grammar_topic: choosing between the gerund and the infinitive
title: Deciding to Change Careers
body: After years of enjoying her stable office job, Malika suddenly decided to quit and open a small bakery instead. Her family avoided discussing it at first, worried she was making a mistake. 'I've finished thinking it over,' she told them firmly, 'I want to try baking professionally.' She admitted risking her savings terrified her, but she refused to keep postponing the decision any longer. Her manager offered to keep her position open for a month, hoping she'd reconsider, but Malika chose to decline politely. She began learning new recipes every evening, practising until midnight some nights. Her brother suggested starting small, selling bread only to neighbours before opening an actual shop. She agreed to try this plan, mostly to avoid disappointing her parents completely. Within weeks, she managed to build a small, loyal group of customers who kept requesting her sourdough specifically. She loves waking up early now, something that used to feel impossible during her office years. Looking back, she remembers hesitating to take the first step for almost a year. Now, kneading dough at dawn, she can't imagine going back to spending sunny afternoons behind a computer screen.

words.context: Keep postponing the decision any longer.
A small, loyal group of customers.
She remembers hesitating to take the first step.

grammar_topic: reported speech: statements and questions
title: The Argument at the Shop
body: The shop assistant told me the jacket couldn't be returned without a receipt, even though I explained I'd lost it somewhere between the till and the bus stop. I said I had bought it only yesterday, and she asked if I remembered the exact time of purchase. I told her I didn't, not precisely, though I insisted the tag was still attached. She said the manager would need to approve any exception personally. When the manager arrived, he asked what the actual problem was, and the assistant explained that I claimed to have lost my receipt. He asked me directly whether I'd paid by card, and I confirmed that I had. He said he could check the payment system instead, which surprised the assistant, who apparently hadn't considered that option. After a brief search, he told her that he'd found my transaction from the previous afternoon. She apologised, saying she hadn't realised there was another way to verify the purchase. The manager reassured me that they'd process the refund immediately. Walking out, I wondered whether shop assistants were ever taught that receipts weren't the only proof that mattered.

words.context: The jacket couldn't be returned without a receipt.
Between the till and the bus stop.
I claimed to have lost my receipt.
He'd found my transaction from the previous afternoon.
Another way to verify the purchase.

grammar_topic: the third conditional
title: If I Had Backed Up My Phone
body: If I had backed up my phone before it fell in the river, I wouldn't have lost four years of photographs in a single afternoon. My friends had warned me repeatedly, but I had always assumed disaster would happen to someone else, not me. If I had listened, I would still have pictures from my sister's wedding, from countless ordinary days I'd never bothered to appreciate until they vanished. The technician tried everything possible, but he said if the phone had spent less time underwater, he might have recovered something. If I hadn't panicked and left it in a bag of rice for a week, perhaps that delay wouldn't have made things worse. My mother, gentler than I deserved, reminded me that if the memories mattered so much, I would have printed at least a few photos over the years. She was right, though it didn't comfort me much at the time. If this hadn't happened, I probably would have continued ignoring backups indefinitely, assuming I had more time than I actually did. Now, painfully, everything is backed up in three different places, a habit I would never have developed without this expensive lesson.

words.context: If I had backed up my phone.
Disaster would happen to someone else.
A habit I would never have developed.

grammar_topic: quantifiers
title: Too Many Chargers
body: Our kitchen drawer contains far too many phone chargers, though barely any of them actually work anymore. There's a little space left for anything else, since old cables have slowly taken over completely. 'How many of these do we actually need?' my husband asks, holding up a tangled handful. Not many, I admit, though somehow we own dozens. A few belong to phones we don't even have anymore, replaced years ago. Little by little, we've collected chargers from every device we've ever owned, unable to throw any away, just in case. There's too much clutter and too little organisation, my husband complains, not entirely unfairly. We spend a little time each weekend meaning to sort it out, though we rarely make much progress. Some chargers fit nothing we currently own; a few might belong to devices that don't even exist anymore. Eventually, we find exactly one charger that works with everything we actually use. The rest, several dozen useless cables, finally go into a bag for recycling. There's much more space in the drawer now, and surprisingly little regret about throwing away years of accumulated, tangled uncertainty.

grammar_topic: relative clauses: defining and non-defining
title: The Case That Puzzled Everyone
body: The detective who was assigned to the case had never seen anything quite like it before. The jewellery shop, which had been robbed twice in the same month, had unusually good security cameras that recorded nothing useful either time. The owner, whose insurance claim seemed suspiciously well prepared, became the detective's first real suspect. Neighbours who worked nearby reported seeing nothing unusual on either occasion. The thief, who apparently knew exactly where the cameras' blind spots were, left almost no evidence behind. A young witness, whose statement initially seemed unreliable, eventually provided the crucial detail that broke the case open. She mentioned a delivery van that had parked outside both times, something nobody else had noticed. The van, which belonged to a small local courier company, led detectives straight to a former employee who still had a set of keys. He was someone whose financial troubles, colleagues later admitted, had been obvious for months. The case, which had frustrated the whole department for weeks, was finally solved through one overlooked detail. The owner, who had genuinely been innocent all along, apologised publicly for the unwanted suspicion he'd briefly faced.

words.context: The detective who was assigned to the case.
Whose insurance claim seemed suspiciously well prepared.
The crucial detail that broke the case open.

grammar_topic: question tags
title: You Haven't Met Yet, Have You?
body: 'You two haven't actually met before, have you?' our host asked, guiding me toward a stranger by the window. 'No, we haven't,' I said, shaking hands with a woman who looked vaguely familiar. 'You work at the university, don't you?' she asked immediately, catching me off guard. 'I do,' I admitted, 'but I don't think we've worked together, have we?' She laughed. 'No, but you gave a lecture I attended once — you don't remember, do you?' I didn't, honestly, though I pretended to for a moment before admitting defeat. 'It wasn't very memorable, was it?' I joked, and she laughed again, more genuinely this time. We talked for a while about mutual acquaintances. 'You know Farrukh, don't you?' she asked. 'Everyone knows Farrukh,' I replied, 'he's impossible to avoid at these parties, isn't he?' By the end of the evening, we'd exchanged numbers, promising to have coffee sometime. 'You will actually call, won't you?' she asked as I left. 'I will,' I said, and surprisingly, for once, I actually meant it. Small parties like this aren't usually my thing, are they, my friends would say — yet somehow, this one turned out rather well.

words.context: You gave a lecture I attended once.
